::: {.decision}
**Your decision.** A merchant sells goods for HK$100,000. Service A settles in bank money today with a 1.5% fee. Service B charges 1% and delivers a redeemable digital balance in 30 days. Which offer has higher value today?
:::

## Translate both offers into cash today

A delivers **HK$98,500** today. Assume the merchant values cash at simple annual interest of 6% on a 360-day basis. If B pays HK$99,000 at par on day 30, its value today is 99,000 / 1.005 = **HK$98,507.46**. The fee advantage just covers the wait.

Suppose that in 1% of cases the redemption pays only 90% of the balance, and otherwise pays in full. Expected redemption becomes 99,000 × 0.999 = HK$98,901. Discounting gives **HK$98,408.96**. A risk-neutral merchant using this forecast prefers A. A merchant with payroll due tomorrow must also check whether it can borrow against the balance.

## How much redemption risk erases the fee saving?


```{=html}
<figure class="ess-figure" data-essentials-figure="payment-value">
<figcaption><strong>Read when the cheaper fee stops paying</strong></figcaption><p>The merchant receives HK$98,500 from A today. B promises HK$99,000 on day 30 and can lose 10% of that balance if redemption falls short. The graph discounts B to today.</p><ol class="professional-timeline"><li><strong>Today</strong>A settles in bank money. B leaves no settlement cash available today.</li><li><strong>Day 30</strong>B redeems at par or delivers a smaller amount under the loss scenario.</li></ol>
<div class="ess-chart"></div>
<p><strong>Read the graph.</strong> How much redemption risk erases B’s advantage? What if payroll is due tomorrow?</p>
<details><summary>Check your reading</summary><p>A probability of about 0.076% is enough under these assumptions. Even at zero redemption risk, B gains only HK$7.46 in present value. Additional payroll funding costs above that amount would favor A.</p></details>
</figure>
```


**How likely can the 10% redemption loss be before A becomes preferable?**

<details><summary>Work through the decision</summary><p>Set 99,000 × (1 − 0.1p) = 98,500 × 1.005. The break-even probability is approximately 0.076%. Ask who owes redemption, when settlement is final, and what cash is available during a delay. The probabilities and terms are illustrative and describe no particular payment instrument.</p></details>


```{=html}
<section aria-label="Practice brief"><h2>Which settlement service should the merchant choose?</h2><details><summary>Compare your recommendation</summary><p>Choose A under the stated 1% probability of a redemption loss. It delivers HK$98,500 today against B’s expected present value of HK$98,408.96. Even certain redemption gives B an advantage of only HK$7.46 in today’s money. If using B creates an additional payroll bridging cost above HK$7.46 in present value, A wins even with full redemption. Ask when the merchant can actually use the funds.</p></details></section>
```


<details class="full-course-detail"><summary>Put payroll and settlement on the same cash schedule</summary><p>An expected settlement value helps rank the options only after the merchant can meet tomorrow’s payroll. Record bank cash available on the payroll date, the amount the bank will advance against the balance, and fees and interest on the bridge. Convert only the incremental bridge cost to today’s value and deduct it from the delayed option when comparing the two.</p></details>
